newsitem.title: UK: Pro-British N.Ireland leader sees fake IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Pro-British N.Ireland leader sees fake IRA truce.

text.p: David Trimble, Northern Ireland's main pro-British politician, said on Thursday that resurgent IRA guerrillas might offer a truce ahead of a spring general election but it would be a phoney bid to win votes.

"At the moment I think it is more likely than not that there will be a tactical manoeuvre immediately before the general election but I don't think there'll be a genuine ceasefire," Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Trimble told Reuters.
Elections must be held in the United Kingdom -- Britain and Northern Ireland -- by May at the latest.

Trimble said in an interview that if the IRA (Irish Republican Army) declared a ceasefire, it would be aimed at winning votes for its political wing Sinn Fein and "wrong- footing" its rival for the pro-Irish vote, the moderate SDLP.
It would also be intended to put an incoming British government "on the spot" about reviving stalled peace efforts.
"If there is any ceasefire before the general election, I don't think it will be a genuine one," Trimble said.
"In fact I think it will be deliberately pitched in terms where it will not be possible for (Prime Minister) John Major, or others, to say it satisfies (them)."

Trimble was speaking some 12 hours after the IRA issued a blunt statement demanding an unconditional seat for Sinn Fein in all-party peace talks and signalling there would be no let-up in an armed campaign to end Britain's rule over Northern Ireland.

Attempts to forge a settlement between the province's majority pro-British Protestants and minority pro-Irish Roman Catholics have been virtually paralysed for the past year with the collapse of an IRA truce and bitter party rivalries.
The security climate worsened recently with pro-British Loyalist extremists suspected of two revenge attacks on Catholics after an escalation in IRA hostilities.

That fuelled fears that a two-year truce by the Loyalists might collapse. The UUP, which speaks for most Protestants, and the SDLP (Social Democratic and Labour Party), the main Catholic group, condemn all violence.
Multi-party talks, which exclude Sinn Fein, resume in Belfast next week chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell.
Trimble said rival Protestant and Catholic parties must reach consensus on guerrilla disarmament - an issue that has blighted the discussions so far - if the talks were to progress.
Britain and the pro-Irish factions are poles apart on the future of the peace process. Major says the militants must call a credible ceasefire before Sinn Fein is allowed into the talks.

Sinn Fein, which got 15.5 per cent support in a province-wide vote last June, says Major is blocking its democratic rights to buy time from key UUP legislators for his threatened government, whose term expires in May.
Trimble, heading a nine-man bloc in Britain's lower house, scoffed at suggestions that he had a king-maker role that could determine whether Major was forced from power before he was ready.

The UUP leader, speaking at UUP headquarters in central Belfast, refused to say how his party would vote in the event of a confidence vote in the British parliament where the ruling Conservatives no longer have an overall majority.
It would consider what was in the best interests of its electorate in British Northern Ireland, he said, but indicated the party would not rush headlong into undermining the current government.

"I have used the phrase (that) we have no intention to act in a capricious or irresponsible manner. We're not going to act irresponsibly. We're not just going to turf the government out just for the hell-of-it."

Trimble, whose UUP has traditionally backed Conservative governments, refused to be drawn on whether opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair would succeed Major and said little appeared to separate the two major parties on Northern Ireland.
"There's no clear blue water between them, is there?" Trimble remarked. "I don't know that there would be a great deal of difference on fundamentals between Conservative and Labour.."
